sources.source: Automating the Detection of Snapshot Isolation Anomalies (Jorwekar et al., 2007)

items.item: the read-only transaction anomaly's own precise definition
Dirty Write (P0) is excluded by ANSI SQL-92 only at its strictest level, but every real locking implementation excludes it unconditionally via row locks.
Dirty Read (P1) is the anomaly ANSI's own definitions state ambiguously: a narrow reading and a broad reading of the same English sentence prohibit genuinely different sets of histories.
Non-repeatable Read (P2) is a special case of Read Skew (A5A) where the two items read are the same single item.

at.step: Reveal: Read Skew and Write Skew

items.item: Phantom (P3) is about a changing set of rows matching a predicate, not a changing value of a single row — a distinct phenomenon from the first three.
Lost Update (P4) silently discards a committed change with no error from the database at all; the application has no way to know, from the database's own response, that this happened.

at.step: Reveal: Lost Update, a real timeline

items.item: Write Skew (A5B) needs two transactions and a cross-row constraint; each transaction, in isolation, looks correct, and the violation only exists across the two commits together.

at.step: Reveal: Read Skew and Write Skew

items.item: The read-only transaction anomaly is the one case where a transaction that writes nothing at all can still see an impossible state, which is why it survives mechanisms (like simple read/write conflict detection) that would otherwise seem to rule it out.

Adya's Direct Serialization Graph turns 'does this history violate isolation' into a checkable graph-cycle question, closing the exact ambiguity Berenson et al.'s own English-language phenomena left open.

at.step: Reveal: Adya's formalization, the real fix

items.item: A two-transaction timeline is the standard way every one of these anomalies is actually shown: two labeled transactions, their reads and writes interleaved in a specific order, with commit points marked.

at.step: Reveal: Lost Update, a real timeline

items.item: Naming an anomaly precisely (not just 'something went wrong with concurrency') is what makes it possible to say which isolation levels prevent it and which don't — the subject of the next two topics.

Serializable, the strictest ANSI level, is defined to prohibit all of A1–A3 (and hence implicitly all of P0–P4), but Berenson et al. note the phenomenon-based approach still leaves the weaker levels ambiguous about exactly which histories they permit.
